Subject: RFI: Reserved capacity guidance for LLM inference workloads

Hi Aisha,

Thanks for taking this. We’re compiling our RFP response checklist and need a clear recommendation from Redwood on a reserved GPU commitment that meets our production targets. High-level profile below: 

- Workload: mixed text generation + embedding store. Generations: user-facing chat (avg prompt+response tokens 600), async batch reranking jobs (large multi-document prompts), embeddings pipeline (1M vectors / month).
- Expected steady-state throughput: 220 qps across chat endpoints during peak (PST), with 95th pct tail latency SLO of <300ms for short-turn prompts (avg 120 tokens).
- Burst profile: up to 2.5x sustained burst for 6–12 hours during product launches.
- Preferred commitment: 12–24 month reservation, budgeted as committed vGPU-hours or committed token units.

Can you provide:
1) A suggested reserved SKU mix (GPU families and counts) by performance tier (baseline / peak / burst) that maps to our throughput and SLOs.
2) Recommended buffer (warm pools / prewarmed slots) sizing to hit tail latency targets.
3) Suggested quantization and batching knobs we should use to reduce committed capacity without impacting 95th tail.
4) A simple workbook (CSV/XLSX) we can use to model cost vs utilization.

Procurement will need these details for our internal scoring matrix. If helpful, we can share anonymized logs from a 2-week beta.

Thanks,
Lucy Nguyen
Senior Procurement Manager

Subject: Internal: sizing notes for DataForge RFI (please review)

Aisha / Lauren — drafting the sizing recommendation below. I’ll format into the workbook after you sign off. Notes are conservative to preserve 95th-tail <300ms for short-turn prompts.

Summary recommended SKU mix (baseline -> peak):
- Baseline pool (steady-state 220 qps): 12 x H100-80GB (packed with model variants): dedicated inference nodes with continuous batching, KV cache enabled for chat sessions. This maps to ~430k vGPU-hours/month (committed).
- Reserve burst runway: additional 6 x A100-80GB as burst lane (prewarmed, autoscale-triggered) to absorb ~2.5x capacity spikes for up to 12 hours.
- Embeddings: 3 x L4 / T4 cost-optimized nodes for high-throughput pairwise encoding (batching nightly jobs). If you want sub-100ms vector latency for retrieval pipelines, consider 2 x medium L4s colocated with main pool.

Rationale and knobs:
- Prewarmed slots: reserve ~10% of baseline as hot slots (we recommend 15% for chat to hit tail SLO) — these are pinned containers with warmed KV caches.
- Batching: use dynamic batching with max batch size 128 for generations; reduce to 32 for low-latency routes. This trades throughput for tail latency; our simulations show 15% cost savings with no tail SLO impact at these batch sizes.
- Quantization: recommend FP16 for H100 baseline; consider 4-bit quantization on non-latency-critical reranking jobs (saves ~2.2x memory footprint).
- Fallback policy: route low-priority reranks to quantized variants during burst to free capacity.

Commit model options:
1) vGPU-hour commit: commit 430k vGPU-hours/month for baseline with a 12-month term; add a 6-month burst buffer that Redwood keeps warm but bills only on consumption beyond baseline.
2) Token-anchored commit: commit to 9B tokens/month for generation+embedding equivalence with dynamic mapping to GPU families. This is noisier but simpler for procurement.

Open items for DataForge: region pinning preferences, max committed spend, ability to accept a mixed-family fallback (e.g., move some H100 load to A100 in emergencies).

I’ll convert these to explicit numbers in the workbook and include a cost delta table.

-Karthik

Only burst-consumed hours are billed against the committed baseline; burst-warm hours are visible in the console and included as a separate audit line item (they are not charged unless consumed in excess of baseline). We’ll include a sample CSV export in the workbook.
- Cross-region availability: H100 is available as an opt-in region for Dedicated; however, availability varies by cloud region. For eu-west-1 we recommend A100 as the primary family; H100 fallback will be treated as a performance-tier failover and may require minor model-variant pinning (we’ll supply a compatibility matrix).

A dedicated burst runway of prewarmed nodes will be maintained to absorb traffic spikes; prewarmed hours are visible in Redwood’s billing analytics and are only charged to the Customer when consumed beyond the committed baseline. Redwood’s routing policy will prefer baseline nodes and automatically fail over to quantized model variants and alternate GPU families (A100) in the event of regional capacity constraints to preserve service availability and tail-latency SLOs."
